claims.text: Integrating DSC, containerless induction levitation, and concurrent optical measurements will determine melting temperature to within ±1%.
The integrated approach will determine enthalpy and entropy of fusion to within ±5%.
The integrated approach will provide high-throughput measurements across a broad range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The proposed specimens are homogenized, high-purity HEAs with minimal preexisting defects.
Heating rates from 50 to 500 K/min under high-purity Ar or He will minimize oxidation and thermal gradients.
Calibration with standard reference materials will isolate instrumental contributions.
Thermograms will accurately capture the onset and completion of melting transitions.
Optical images can correlate latent heat with density or volume changes during melting.
Containerless processing avoids container-induced heterogeneous nucleation.
DSC records endothermic melting peaks that provide melting-temperature measurements.
Integration of the DSC melting peak provides the enthalpy of fusion.
Entropy of fusion can be calculated as ΔS = ΔH/Tm.
Containerless induction levitation minimizes contact effects that could skew melting measurements.
Calibrated optical imaging can capture density variations and thereby infer volume change at melting.
The calibration protocol will decouple extrinsic measurement effects from intrinsic material properties.
Conventional container-based calorimetry suffers from substrate-induced errors and inconsistent thermal gradients.
Those container-related effects cause larger uncertainties for compositionally complex alloys.
The approach is applicable to HEAs compositionally similar to AlCoCrFeNi over a wide range of liquidus temperatures.
Extremely high-temperature HEAs or HEAs with rapid kinetic effects may require additional calibration.
A deviation greater than 10% between optically estimated volume change and independent density measurements constitutes failure of the volume-change target.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator describes latent heat being released during melting, whereas the mechanism correctly characterizes melting as an endothermic DSC event, implying heat absorption.
